topic: margin of error and sampling inference
problem: A researcher selected a random sample of 400 adults from a certain city and found that 62% of the adults in the sample support building a new park. The margin of error associated with this estimate is 4.8%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Exactly 62% of all adults in the city support building the new park.
It is plausible that between 57.2% and 66.8% of all adults in the city support building the new park.
Between 57.2% and 66.8% of the 400 adults in the sample support building the new park.
It is plausible that between 57.2% and 66.8% of all adults in the state support building the new park.
correctAnswer: It is plausible that between 57.2% and 66.8% of all adults in the city support building the new park.

bad.why: The margin of error is already given; recomputing it with a confidence-interval formula is unneeded and that formula is not on the SAT reference sheet.
There is no data list to analyze; mean or standard deviation functions cannot interpret what a margin of error says about a population.

algebraFirst.description: Computes 62 - 4.8 and 62 + 4.8, then must still decide which group the interval describes; generic solvers sometimes recompute the margin with 1.96*sqrt(p(1-p)/n) instead of interpreting it.

explanationNotes: Explain margin of error in plain words: the sample's 62% could be off by up to 4.8 percentage points, so the percent for the whole population that was sampled (adults in this city) is plausibly between 57.2% and 66.8%. Point out that the sample itself is exactly 62%, and the result cannot be stretched to a population that was never sampled, such as the whole state.
notes: Verified: 62 - 4.8 = 57.2 and 62 + 4.8 = 66.8; three choices share that interval, so the decision is the interpretation (population vs sample vs unsampled population), not the arithmetic. 1.96*sqrt(0.62*0.38/400) = 4.76%, consistent with the stated 4.8%.
